summary.en: Rome grew from a city in central Italy into an empire around the whole Mediterranean. The group on the map comprises the kingdom, the republic, the empire and its eastern continuation, the Byzantine Empire, which together span more than two millennia.

text.en: According to tradition Rome was founded about 753 BC on the river Tiber in central Italy. The kingdom (about 753–509 BC) was followed by the republic (about 509–27 BC) and by the empire from 27 BC. Little is known with certainty about the time of the kings, since the accounts are largely based on oral tradition.

The empire was divided several times. The Western Roman Empire fell in 476, when Romulus Augustus was deposed by Odoacer. The Eastern Roman Empire, which has afterwards been called the Byzantine Empire, remained until the Ottomans conquered Constantinople in 1453. The inhabitants themselves called their empire Roman.
Rome. Constantine the Great moved the imperial seat to Byzantium in 330 and renamed the city Constantinople, which was then the capital in the east until 1453.

Romulus (the first king according to tradition), Augustus (the first emperor, from 27 BC), Trajan (98–117), Constantine the Great (306–337, the first Christian emperor) and Justinian I (527–565) in Byzantium.

The empire was at its largest under Trajan, about 5 million km² in the year 117 according to the estimate in Wikipedia's fact box. The Byzantine Empire was at its largest under Justinian I, who for a short time recovered large parts of Italy and the coasts of the western Mediterranean.

Latin, and with time increasingly Greek. In Byzantium Greek replaced Latin as the official language. Roman polytheism with the imperial cult, and from 380 Nicene Christianity as the official religion.

The eagle, the aquila, was one of Rome's most prominent emblems, above all as the legions' field standard. Each legion had one eagle, and losing it was regarded as a great disgrace. According to Pliny the Elder the eagle was kept as the only standard after 104 BC, but other sources show that the legions still used other animals for some time after that. The map shows the eagle for the whole group except the Byzantine Empire, which has a symbol of its own.
The kings are overthrown and the republic is introduced, according to the traditional dating. Rome then rules only the area closest to the city.

mapNote.en: On the map the republic begins in 501 BC, and the kingdom is shown in parallel until 482 BC.

text.en: In the century after the Gauls' sack of Rome, the city has conquered most of Italy. Now a war against Carthage over Sicily begins, which lasts for 23 years. When Carthage is defeated in 241 BC, Sicily becomes Rome's first province, and soon afterwards Rome also takes Sardinia from Carthage.

mapNote.en: The map shows steady growth during the first years of the war and no clear step in 241 BC.

text.en: Rome defeats Hannibal and Carthage at Zama in the Second Punic War. In the peace the year after, Carthage loses its territories outside Africa, and in the decades after that Rome becomes the leading power in the Mediterranean.

mapNote.en: The map shows great growth in 203–199 BC and then a decrease of about a third from 198 BC.

text.en: In the Third Punic War Rome destroys the city of Carthage, and Carthage's land becomes the province of Africa. The same year Corinth is destroyed, and Greece and Macedonia become provinces ruled directly from Rome.

Julius Caesar conquers Gaul, roughly present-day France, Belgium and Switzerland. The decisive battle is at Alesia in 52 BC. The wars give Caesar wealth and prestige, and they lead to the civil war that ends the republic.

mapNote.en: The map shows the whole of Gaul as Roman from 51 BC. According to the source Gaul became a province only in 27 BC.

text.en: Octavian's fleet defeats Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC. The year after, Ptolemaic Egypt is conquered, and Antony and Cleopatra take their own lives. With that a long series of civil wars ends.
The Senate gives Octavian the title Augustus. He is regarded as the first Roman emperor.
The empire is at its largest under Trajan, about 5 million km².

During the crisis of the 3rd century, with civil wars, invasions and plague, Emperor Valerian is taken prisoner by the Sasanians in 260. The same year Gaul, Britain and Hispania break away as the Gallic Empire, and in 267 the eastern provinces become the Palmyrene Empire. Aurelian defeats both and has united the empire again by 274.

mapNote.en: The map shows the split from 261, when the area shrinks by about 40 per cent, and the reunification in two steps, 270 and 283.

text.en: Constantine the Great moves the imperial seat to Byzantium, which is given the name Constantinople.

Since 395 the empire has been divided into a western and an eastern half, and in large parts of the west new kingdoms have taken power. The Western Roman Empire falls when Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustus. The Eastern Roman Empire lives on.

mapNote.en: The map shows the Western Roman Empire up to and including 475.

text.en: Justinian I tries to take back the west. The general Belisarius defeats the Vandal kingdom in North Africa in 533 and then attacks Italy, where the Ostrogothic kingdom is largely finished by 554. Under Justinian the empire is at its largest in Byzantine times.

After a long war against Persia (602–628) the empire is exhausted. The Rashidun Caliphate conquers Syria in 634–638, and at the river Yarmuk the Byzantine army is annihilated. Egypt too is lost for good. When Heraclius dies in 641 the empire has lost its rich eastern provinces and up to three quarters of its revenues.

mapNote.en: The map shows the losses in steps from 638 to 647.

text.en: The Seljuks win a decisive victory at Manzikert and take Emperor Romanos IV prisoner. The same year Bari, the empire's last city in Italy, falls to the Normans. During a decade of civil strife Turkish forces take large parts of Anatolia, all the way to the Sea of Marmara. With the help of the First Crusade Alexios I later recovers parts of western Anatolia.

mapNote.en: The map shows the loss in Anatolia from 1085, when the area is halved, and some recovered land from 1099.

text.en: The Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople and the empire is split up. The city is retaken in 1261, but after that the empire is only a regional power.

mapNote.en: The map shows almost no area for the empire in 1206–1226 and none at all in 1227–1278. Nicaea, where the empire lived on and which retook Constantinople in 1261, is not included in the map data for the empire. From 1279 the empire is visible again.

text.en: The Ottomans conquer Constantinople, and the Byzantine Empire ceases to exist.

mapNote.en: The map shows a very small remnant of the empire up to and including 1474.

The sources give about 753 BC to 1453. The last years of the map, up to 1474, show only a small remnant of Byzantium. Cliopatria states that the Seleucid Empire was subordinate to the Roman Republic in 204–190 BC, but this is contradicted by the sources: Rome and the Seleucid Empire were at war in 192–188 BC and made peace at Apamea in 188 BC. It is therefore not shown as influence.

summary.en: The Achaemenid Empire was an ancient Iranian empire founded by Cyrus the Great. It was the largest empire of its time and stretched from the Balkans and Cyrenaica in the west to the Indus Valley in the east.

text.en: In 550 BC, starting from Persis in the south-west of the Iranian Plateau. Cyrus the Great defeated Media, Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

Alexander the Great conquered the whole empire in a campaign that began in 336 BC and was complete in 330 BC. After Alexander's death in 323 BC most of the old empire came under the Seleucid Empire and the Ptolemaic Kingdom.
Several: Babylon, Pasargadae (under Cyrus the Great) and Susa (under Darius the Great). Ecbatana and Persepolis were ceremonial capitals.
Cyrus the Great (559–530 BC), Cambyses II (530–522 BC), Darius the Great (522–486 BC), Xerxes I (486–465 BC) and the last, Darius III (336–330 BC).
About 5.5 million km² around 500 BC, according to Wikipedia's fact box.

Old Persian was the language of the dynasty and Aramaic the official language of the administration. Zoroastrianism was the state religion, but many other religions existed in the empire. The empire is known for its administration, the Royal Road, an organised postal system and religious tolerance, especially under Cyrus.

The royal field standard of the Achaemenids. Xenophon describes the standard that Artaxerxes II carried at Cunaxa as a golden eagle with outspread wings on a long spear shaft, and the same standard is said to have been used by Cyrus the Great. What it looked like in detail is not known; the drawing is a simplification of the description.
Cyrus the Great of the Achaemenid dynasty founds the empire, with a base on the Iranian plateau. In 547 BC he conquers Lydia in Anatolia.

mapNote.en: The map begins in 551 BC and shows the empire already then with about 3.3 million km².

text.en: Cyrus conquers Babylonia.

mapNote.en: The map shows the growth from 541 BC.

text.en: Cambyses II, Cyrus's son, defeats Pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium and conquers Egypt. The Libyans and the Greeks in Cyrene submit without a fight.

mapNote.en: The map shows the growth in a period beginning in 531 BC.

title.en: Darius I: the empire at its largest

text.en: Darius I takes power after fighting over the throne. Under him the empire reaches its greatest extent, about 5.5 million km², from the Balkans and Cyrenaica in the west to the Indus Valley in the east. From 513 BC the Persians bring Thrace under their rule, and Macedonia becomes a vassal state.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire at its largest, about 5.6 million km², from 501 BC.

text.en: The Persians try to conquer the Greek mainland. They are defeated at Marathon in 490 BC and after Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 BC. After the losses the Persians withdraw from Europe, and Macedonia and the Ionian cities become independent again.

mapNote.en: The map shows no decrease after the wars: the area is the same in 501–406 BC.

text.en: When Darius II dies, the Egyptian rebel leader Amyrtaeus takes the opportunity to throw off Persian rule. An attempt to retake Egypt in 373 BC fails.
Artaxerxes III conquers Egypt again, after Pharaoh Nectanebo II has been defeated and fled south.

mapNote.en: The map shows the reconquest only from 338 BC.

text.en: Alexander the Great crosses into Asia and defeats the Persians at the Granicus in 334, Issus in 333 and Gaugamela in 331 BC. King Darius III flees from the two latter battles.
Persepolis is burned, and Darius III is killed by his own satrap Bessus. Alexander has conquered the whole empire and places it under the Macedonian Empire.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire, with a decreasing area, up to and including 328 BC.
The source gives 550–330 BC.

summary.en: Macedonia was an ancient kingdom in the north-eastern part of the Greek peninsula. Under Philip II it became the leading power in Greece, and his son Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire all the way to the river Indus.

text.en: Probably in the 7th century BC, according to legend founded by Caranus or Perdiccas I. Before the 4th century BC it was a small kingdom, and for a time it was subject to the Persian Empire, first as a vassal and then as part of the empire until 479 BC.

Alexander's empire was divided after his death in 323 BC, but Macedonia remained as a kingdom. Rome abolished the monarchy after the Third Macedonian War in 168 BC. A brief revival in 150–148 BC ended with Macedonia becoming a Roman province.
Aigai until 399 BC, then Pella.
Philip II (359–336 BC), Alexander the Great (336–323 BC), Cassander (305–297 BC), Philip V (221–179 BC) and the last king, Perseus (179–168 BC).
About 5.2 million km² in 323 BC, when Alexander died, according to Wikipedia's fact box.
Ancient Macedonian, Attic Greek and Koine Greek. Greek polytheism and Hellenistic religion. Alexander's teacher Aristotle gained great influence on Western philosophy.

The Vergina Sun, a sun with sixteen rays. It is found on the golden chest in a royal tomb from the 4th century BC at Aigai (Vergina), which belonged to either Philip II, Alexander's father, or Philip III. Scholars disagree about whether it was the Macedonian royal house's own emblem or only a common Greek decorative motif.

Philip II becomes king. With a reformed army, in which the phalanxes carry long pikes, he brings the Greek mainland, Paeonia and the Thracian Odrysian kingdom under his rule through war and diplomacy.
Philip II defeats Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea. He then founds the League of Corinth of Greek states, which Macedonia leads.

Philip II is murdered, and the army proclaims his son Alexander king. Alexander puts down the Greeks' revolt, destroys Thebes in 335 BC and is chosen leader of the planned attack on the Persian Empire.
Alexander defeats the Persians at the Granicus in 334, Issus in 333 and Gaugamela in 331 BC. In 330 BC Darius III is killed by his satrap Bessus, and Alexander takes over the Persian Empire.

mapNote.en: The map shows Alexander's conquests only from 324 BC. In 332–325 BC it shows only a small area, about 0.2 million km².

text.en: Alexander defeats King Porus at the river Hydaspes in present-day Punjab. The empire now stretches from Greece and Egypt across Mesopotamia and Persia to Central Asia and present-day Pakistan.
Alexander dies in Babylon without a designated heir. During the wars between his generals, the Diadochi, the empire is divided up.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire with about 4.7–4.8 million km² from 324 to 309 BC, that is also the years after Alexander's death.

text.en: Alexander's son Alexander IV has been killed in 311 or 310 BC. In 306–305 BC the generals proclaim themselves kings in their territories. At Ipsus in 301 BC Antigonus, who had tried to build up a large empire, falls, and the victors divide his land between them. With that Alexander's empire is finally divided up.

mapNote.en: The map shows the decrease in two steps, from 308 and from 302 BC, when the empire is down to about 0.15 million km².

text.en: Rome defeats King Perseus at Pydna in the Third Macedonian War. The monarchy is abolished, and Macedonia is divided into four republics under Rome.

mapNote.en: The map data for the empire ends in 293 BC.
The map data ends in 293 BC, but according to the source the kingdom remained until 168 BC.

summary.en: The Han dynasty was an imperial dynasty in China, founded by Liu Bang. It is regarded as a golden age in Chinese history, and the majority people of present-day China still call themselves Han.

text.en: Liu Bang was proclaimed emperor in 202 BC, after the Battle of Gaixia. The dynasty followed the short-lived Qin dynasty. It is divided into the Western Han (202 BC–9 AD) and the Eastern Han (25–220), with the Xin dynasty (9–23), which the regent Wang Mang founded, in between.

After the year 92 the court eunuchs gained ever more power, and large Daoist movements started revolts, among them the Yellow Turban Rebellion. The empire was divided among warlords, and the dynasty ended in 220, when Cao Pi of Wei took the throne from Emperor Xian. The Three Kingdoms period then followed.
Chang'an (206 BC–9 AD and 190–195), Luoyang (23–190 and 196) and Xuchang (196–220).
Emperor Gaozu, that is Liu Bang (202–195 BC), Emperor Wu (141–87 BC), Emperor Xuan (74–48 BC), Emperor Guangwu (25–57) and the last, Emperor Xian (189–220).

An estimated 6 million km² around 50 BC (Western Han) and about 6.5 million km² around the year 100 (Eastern Han), according to Wikipedia's fact box. The census in 2 AD gave about 57.7 million inhabitants.

Language: Old Chinese. From Emperor Wu the court officially supported Confucianism in education and politics. Under the Han, papermaking and seismometers were invented. The campaigns against the Xiongnu gave the Han control of the Hexi Corridor and the Tarim Basin, which helped the Silk Road to emerge.
Liu Bang is proclaimed emperor. The Han dynasty begins.
Emperor Wu begins a series of campaigns against the Xiongnu.
The Han drive the Xiongnu out of a large area from the Hexi Corridor to Lop Nur. In 111 BC four new border prefectures are established there, settled with soldier-colonists.

mapNote.en: The map shows the growth only from 110 BC.

title.en: Conquests in the south and in Korea

text.en: The Han conquer Gojoseon on the Korean Peninsula, after having taken Nanyue (111 BC) and Dian (109 BC) in the south.

After fighting with the Xiongnu over the oasis cities of the Tarim Basin from about 115 BC, the Han set up a protectorate over the Western Regions. It is the first time a Chinese government rules the area directly.

mapNote.en: The map shows the growth in the period from 50 BC.

text.en: The regent Wang Mang takes power and founds the Xin dynasty. The Han are restored in 25 as the Eastern Han.

mapNote.en: The map shows almost no area for the Han Empire in 6–13 and none at all in 14–29. The Eastern Han is visible from the year 30.

text.en: The Han defeat the Northern Xiongnu at Ikh Bayan in 89, and in 91 they flee to the Ili Valley. The same year the office of Protector of the Western Regions is established again, with Ban Chao in the post.
A large uprising is put down within a year, but the generals who fought against it keep their armies and build up power of their own as imperial authority falls apart.

mapNote.en: The map shows the decrease only from 197 and more sharply from 207.

text.en: The warlord Cao Cao loses the naval battle at Red Cliffs and cannot take the land south of the Yangtze. China is divided into three spheres of power: Cao Cao in the north, Sun Quan in the south and Liu Bei in the west.
Cao Pi takes the throne from Emperor Xian, and the Han dynasty ends. The Three Kingdoms period begins.

mapNote.en: The source gives 202 BC–220 AD.

summary.en: The Maurya Empire was a great power in South Asia with its power base in Magadha on the Ganges plain. Much of what we know comes from the edicts of Ashoka, inscriptions spread across South Asia, and from surviving parts of Megasthenes's lost historical work.

text.en: Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire around 320 BC (the fact box says about 321 BC) after he had defeated the Nanda dynasty. He extended his rule westward to Afghanistan south of the Hindu Kush and southward to the northern Deccan.
The empire was held loosely together until 185 BC, when the last emperor, Brihadratha, was murdered by Pushyamitra Shunga.
Pataliputra, near present-day Patna.
Chandragupta (about 321–298 BC), Bindusara (298–272 BC) and Ashoka (about 268–232 BC).

Under Ashoka, when the empire for a short time ruled the great cities and main roads of the whole subcontinent except the far south. The source gives no area. Outside the core areas the empire's extent depended on how loyal the local commanders were.

Ashoka became a Buddhist after the violent Kalinga War and sent missionaries to, among other places, Sri Lanka and Central Asia, which contributed to Buddhism becoming a world religion. The population of South Asia in the period is estimated at 15–30 million. Language: Magadhi Prakrit, and probably Sanskrit in literature. Ashoka's lion capital at Sarnath became India's state emblem in 1947.

The lion capital from Sarnath, the top of a pillar that Emperor Ashoka had erected about 250 BC: four lions back to back on a round plate. The lions are interpreted, among other things, as a sign of Ashoka's power. The capital is the model for today's Indian state emblem. The drawing shows the lions and the plate, not the wheel that once sat on top.

Chandragupta Maurya defeats the Nanda dynasty and founds the empire, with his power base in Magadha. His rule reaches westward to Afghanistan south of the Hindu Kush and southward to the northern Deccan.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire from 319 BC.

text.en: Seleucus I, who rules the Asian part of Alexander's former empire, crosses the Indus and meets Chandragupta. They conclude an alliance sealed by marriage: Seleucus hands over his easternmost provinces, among them Gandhara, and receives 500 war elephants. The sources date the conflict differently, to 305–303 or 303–302 BC.

Chandragupta's son Bindusara becomes emperor and extends the empire southward, to present-day Karnataka. Almost the whole Indian peninsula is under him, except the Tamil kingdoms in the far south and Kalinga on the east coast.

mapNote.en: The map shows a large growth, close to 50 per cent, from 292 BC.

text.en: Ashoka, Chandragupta's grandson, becomes emperor. Under him the empire for a short time controls the most important cities and roads of the whole subcontinent except the far south. The source gives 272 BC elsewhere as the beginning of his reign.

Ashoka conquers Kalinga on the east coast, in present-day Odisha. An estimated 100,000 soldiers and civilians are killed. After the devastation Ashoka turns to Buddhism and distances himself from war, but Kalinga remains part of the empire.

mapNote.en: The map shows only a small increase, about 3 per cent, from 257 BC.

text.en: After Ashoka's death a series of weaker emperors follows. The empire loses many areas under his grandson Dasharatha. Some are retaken by Samprati, but after that the empire shrinks step by step.

mapNote.en: The map shows a decrease of about 70 per cent from 226 BC.

text.en: The last emperor, Brihadratha, is murdered by his general Pushyamitra Shunga, who founds the Shunga Empire. The source gives 185 BC, but in one place 180 BC.

mapNote.en: The map shows a greatly reduced empire up to and including 172 BC.
The source gives about 320 to 185 BC.

summary.en: The Ottoman Empire had its centre in present-day Turkey and from the 14th century to the early 20th century ruled large parts of South-Eastern Europe, Western Asia and North Africa. For six centuries it stood at the centre of contacts between the Middle East and Europe.

text.en: From a small principality (beylik) in north-western Anatolia, founded around 1299 by the Turkmen chieftain Osman I. His successors conquered most of Anatolia and reached the Balkans in the middle of the 14th century.

The empire entered the First World War on the side of the Central Powers, and during the war the regime committed genocide against Armenians, Assyrians and Greeks. After the war the empire was occupied and divided by the Allies. After the Turkish War of Independence under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk the sultanate was abolished in 1922, and the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on 29 October 1923.
Söğüt (from about 1299), Nicaea/İznik (1331–1335), Bursa (1335–1360s), Edirne (1360s–1453) and Constantinople/Istanbul (1453–1922). When Edirne was conquered is disputed, between 1361 and 1369.

Osman I (about 1299–1323/24), Mehmed II, who conquered Constantinople in 1453, Selim I, whose conquests led to the sultans taking the title of caliph, Suleiman the Magnificent in the 16th century and the last sultan, Mehmed VI (1918–1922).

About 5.2 million km² in 1683 according to Wikipedia's fact box (3.4 million km² in 1521 and 2.55 million in 1913). That same year, 1683, the empire lost at the Second Siege of Vienna, and scholars usually see that as the beginning of the decline.

Ottoman Turkish was the official language. Arabic, Persian, Greek and many other languages were also used. Sunni Islam was the state religion. The empire's religious communities (millet) were allowed, to varying degrees, to manage their own affairs.

The tughra, the sultan's calligraphic signature. It was put on all official documents and stamped on coins. Each sultan had his own tughra, and the first date from the 14th century (the first Ottoman tughra is Orhan's, 1326). The form is recognised by two loops on the left, three vertical strokes in the middle and two extended lines to the right.
Osman I founds a principality in north-western Anatolia.

Timur defeats the Ottomans at Ankara and takes Sultan Bayezid I prisoner. The empire collapses into a civil war between the sultan's sons that lasts until 1413, and territories in the Balkans, among them Thessaloniki, are lost. They are retaken by Murad II between the 1430s and the 1450s.

mapNote.en: The map (Cliopatria) shows almost no decrease in 1402, only about 4 per cent. The civil war does not show up as lost land.

text.en: Mehmed II conquers Constantinople, which becomes the capital. The Byzantine Empire ceases to exist. The Ottomans already ruled almost all the land around the city.

mapNote.en: The area on the map hardly changes in 1453, since the city was already surrounded by Ottoman land. The map shows the great growth only in 1459–1474.

text.en: Selim I defeats the Mamluks and takes Syria, Egypt and the Hejaz. The empire now reaches the Red Sea, and after the conquests the sultans take the title of caliph.

mapNote.en: On the map the conquest shows up only in 1519, when the area more than doubles.

text.en: The empire is at its largest but loses at the Second Siege of Vienna. A league of European states counterattacks in a war that lasts until 1699.

mapNote.en: According to the source the empire is at its largest in 1683, about 5.2 million km². The map shows the largest area in 1588–1608, about 4.3 million km², and about 3.6 million km² in 1683.

text.en: The war that began at Vienna ends in defeat. The empire cedes most of Hungary, Croatia and Slavonia to the Habsburgs, Podolia to Poland-Lithuania and the Morea and Dalmatia to Venice. These are the empire's first major land losses in Europe.

mapNote.en: The map shows only a small decrease in 1687–1705, a few per cent.

text.en: After the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, Romania, Serbia and Montenegro are recognised as independent. Austria-Hungary occupies Bosnia and Herzegovina, Britain takes over Cyprus and Bulgaria becomes a nearly independent principality.
The Young Turk Revolution restores constitutional monarchy.

title.en: Defeat in the First World War

text.en: The empire has lost large parts of the Middle East during the war, among other things through the Arab Revolt, which drove the Ottomans out of most of the Hejaz and took Damascus. In the Armistice of Mudros the Ottomans give up their garrisons outside Anatolia, and Istanbul is occupied.

mapNote.en: The map shows the large losses in 1917 and 1919.

text.en: The sultanate is abolished. The Republic of Turkey is proclaimed the following year.

mapNote.en: The source gives about 1299 as the start. The map ends in 1923, the year the republic was proclaimed, but the sultanate was abolished as early as 1922.

summary.en: The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous empire in history. It arose in present-day Mongolia and at its largest stretched from the Sea of Japan to Eastern Europe. The group on the map also includes the four khanates into which the empire was divided.

text.en: Temüjin united the nomadic tribes of Mongolia, and a council meeting proclaimed him in 1206 ruler of all Mongols, with the title Genghis Khan. The empire grew rapidly under him and his descendants.

Struggles over the succession split the empire. When Kublai Khan died in 1294 it had been divided into four khanates: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty in China. The Ilkhanate fell apart in 1335–1353, and the Yuan lost China in 1368. The Golden Horde's rule over Eastern Europe is usually counted as ending in 1480, and the Chagatai Khanate remained until 1687.
Avarga (1206–1235) and Karakorum (1235–1271). The Yuan dynasty ruled from Dadu, present-day Beijing.
Genghis Khan (1206–1227), Ögedei (1229–1241), Güyük (1246–1248), Möngke (1251–1259) and Kublai (1260–1294, then Great Khan over the whole empire in name only).
About 23.5 million km² in 1294 according to Wikipedia's fact box, compared with about 4 million km² in 1206 and 13.5 million km² in 1227.

Languages: Middle Mongol, Turkic languages, Chinese, Persian and others. The empire linked East and West, and the enforced peace, the Pax Mongolica, made trade and the exchange of technology and ideas possible across Eurasia.

The tug or sülde, a pole with horsehair in a wreath at the top. It was carried under the Mongol Empire: white banners were used in peacetime and black ones in war. The horsehair alludes to how important horses were to the Mongols.
Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan, ruler of all Mongols.

After bringing Qara Khitai under their rule, the Mongols attack the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia, with severe devastation. The conquest completes the Mongol conquest of Central Asia and begins the conquest of Persia.
Genghis Khan dies. The empire is then about 13.5 million km² and stretches from the Pacific Ocean to the Caspian Sea.
Ögedei's armies take the Jin capital Kaifeng in 1232, and the Jin dynasty in northern China falls in 1234, with help from the Song dynasty.

mapNote.en: The map shows the growth only in the period from 1236.

text.en: The Mongols have conquered almost the whole of Kievan Rus' in 1237–1240 and defeat the Hungarians at the river Sajó in April 1241. When news of the Great Khan Ögedei's death arrives, the army withdraws the following year. Scholars doubt that the death was the only reason: climate and Europe's castles also played a part.
When the caliph refuses to submit, Hulagu's army besieges and conquers Baghdad and plunders the city. The Abbasid Caliphate comes to an end, and the road to Syria lies open.

After the death of Möngke Khan the brothers Kublai and Ariq Böke fight for power. The same year a Mongol army is defeated by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut, and the Mongols never get further than Syria in the Middle East.
The Song imperial family surrenders in 1276, and the last loyalists are defeated in the naval battle of Yamen in 1279. The Yuan dynasty under Kublai Khan now rules all of China.
Kublai Khan dies. The empire has been divided into four khanates.
The Yuan dynasty loses China to the Ming dynasty.

mapNote.en: The map also shows the khanates and therefore runs longer. The source gives 1206–1368 for the Mongol Empire itself.

summary.en: The British Empire consisted of dominions, colonies, protectorates, mandates and other territories governed by Britain and its predecessors. It grew through trade, colonisation and conquest, and at its largest it was the largest empire in history.

text.en: With England's possessions and trading posts overseas in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, and Scotland's attempts to found colonies in the 17th century. Wars against the Netherlands and France made Britain the leading colonial power in North America.

After the Second World War most of the territories gained their independence. India, the most valuable and most populous possession, became independent in 1947. The Suez Crisis in 1956 confirmed the decline, and for many the handover of Hong Kong to China on 1 July 1997 marks the end of the empire. Fourteen British Overseas Territories remain.
London. The British Parliament was the highest legislative power for all possessions.

India was conquered step by step, from the East India Company's victory at Plassey in 1757 to the victory over the Maratha Empire in 1818. Through its dominance of world trade and the seas Britain also in practice governed the economy of areas such as Asia and Latin America. White settler colonies gained increasing self-government and became dominions.

Shortly after the First World War: about 35.5 million km² in 1920, roughly 24 per cent of the Earth's land area. In 1913 about 412 million people lived in the empire, roughly 23 per cent of the world's population.
Called “the empire on which the sun never sets”. The legacy in forms of government, law and language remains in large parts of the world, and many former colonies joined the Commonwealth of Nations.

The crown stands for the monarch as the ultimate source of the state's power. The heraldic crown in Tudor style from 1901 was made uniform across the whole British Empire and is found on many official emblems, in Britain and in the former empire. As early as 1880 the heraldic crown was given rounder arches, after Victoria had become Empress of India.

title.en: Great Britain and the first colonies

text.en: England and Scotland are united as Great Britain. The empire had begun to take shape in the early 17th century, with English settlements in North America and the Caribbean and trading companies such as the East India Company, which managed colonies and trade.

mapNote.en: The map shows almost no area in 1706–1708. The colonies' land shows up only from 1709.

text.en: The Peace of Utrecht ends the War of the Spanish Succession. Britain gets Newfoundland and Acadia from France and Gibraltar and Minorca from Spain, and in addition the right to sell enslaved Africans in Spanish America.

The East India Company defeats the Nawab of Bengal and his French allies. The Company takes control of Bengal and becomes a major military and political power in India, and then expands its territory step by step.
After the Seven Years' War Britain gets New France (Canada) and Florida. France's time as a colonial power in North America is largely over, and Britain is the world's most powerful naval power.

mapNote.en: The map shows the growth from 1762.

text.en: The colonists objected to Parliament in London governing and taxing them without their consent, and war broke out in 1775. At the Peace of Paris in 1783 the independence of the United States is recognised. After that the empire turns more towards Asia, the Pacific and later Africa.

mapNote.en: The map shows the decrease already from 1775, when the war began.

title.en: Largest after the First World War

text.en: Through the Treaty of Versailles Britain gets mandates over, among others, Palestine, Transjordan, Iraq and Tanganyika, former German and Ottoman territories. The empire is at its largest, about 35.5 million km².

mapNote.en: The map shows the largest area in 1918–1931, about 29 million km², and almost a halving from 1932.

text.en: After the Second World War Britain is almost bankrupt, and anti-colonial movements grow. India is partitioned, and India and Pakistan become independent on 15 August 1947, as part of a larger decolonisation.

Prime Minister Macmillan speaks in 1960 of the winds of change in Africa and wants to avoid colonial wars. Decolonisation moves fast: in the 1960s almost ten times as many colonies become independent as in the 1950s.

mapNote.en: The map shows the large decreases in 1956–1968.

text.en: Hong Kong is handed over to China, for many the end of the empire. Most of the colony had been leased for 99 years from 1898.

mapNote.en: The source has the empire begin in the late 16th century and mentions 1997 as the end for many.

summary.en: Ancient Egypt had its centre in the Nile Valley. The group on the map shows the three periods called kingdoms: the Old Kingdom, the age of the pyramid builders, the Middle Kingdom, when the land was united again after a time of fragmentation, and the New Kingdom, when Egypt was at its most powerful and ruled far into the Levant and Nubia. Between the kingdoms lay times of fragmentation.

text.en: The Old Kingdom is most often counted from the Third Dynasty, about 2686 BC, when King Djoser began building in stone at Saqqara. The New Kingdom began about 1570 BC with Ahmose I, who drove out the Hyksos, a people who had ruled northern Egypt. The sources differ about the beginning of the Old Kingdom: World History Encyclopedia counts from the Fourth Dynasty, about 2613 BC.

Under the Sixth Dynasty the regional governors became increasingly independent. After Pepi II's very long reign civil war followed, and a drought around 2200–2150 BC prevented the Nile's floods. The Old Kingdom ended about 2181 BC. The New Kingdom was weakened by attacks from Libyans and the Sea Peoples and by the growing power of the priests of Amun, and ended about 1069 BC.
The Old Kingdom: Memphis. The New Kingdom: Thebes, under Akhenaten Amarna (about 1352–1336 BC), under Ramesses II Pi-Ramesses and afterwards Memphis.
The Old Kingdom: Djoser, Sneferu, Cheops (2589–2566 BC), Khafre and Menkaure. The New Kingdom: Ahmose I, Hatshepsut, Thutmose III (about 1479–1425 BC), Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II.

The New Kingdom was at its largest after Thutmose III's campaigns, which reached from the Euphrates to Nubia. The source gives no area. Under the Old Kingdom Egypt comprised the Nile Valley up to Elephantine, Sinai and the oases of the western desert, and ruled Nubia up to the area north of the Third Cataract.
Egyptian and ancient Egyptian religion. During the Amarna period Akhenaten worshipped the sun disc Aten as his god, something that is often interpreted as the first example of monotheism in history.
The Old Kingdom is called the age of the pyramids: Cheops had the Great Pyramid built at Giza. The terms Old and New Kingdom were coined in 1845 by the German scholar Christian von Bunsen.

The double crown, the pschent, worn by the pharaohs. It united the white crown of Upper Egypt with the red crown of Lower Egypt and stood for the pharaoh's power over the whole united land. The first pharaoh shown with it is Djet in the First Dynasty. No crown has survived; it is known from statues, images and inscriptions. The crown also bore a cobra and a vulture that stood for two goddesses; they are not included in the map's drawing.
Djoser becomes king and begins the Third Dynasty. His architect Imhotep is regarded as the creator of the step pyramid at Saqqara and of building in stone.

mapNote.en: The map shows the Old Kingdom from 2501 BC, with the same border throughout.

text.en: Under the Fourth Dynasty the Old Kingdom reaches its peak. Sneferu already rules from Libya to Sinai and Nubia, and his son Cheops has the Great Pyramid built at Giza.
The governors of the provinces have taken ever more power, and after Pepi II's death civil war follows. A drought prevents the Nile's floods, and the land is struck by famine.

mapNote.en: The map shows the Old Kingdom up to and including 2202 BC.

text.en: Mentuhotep II becomes king in Thebes and then unites all of Egypt again after a time of fragmentation. He is therefore regarded as the founder of the Middle Kingdom.

mapNote.en: The map shows the Middle Kingdom from 2001 BC.

text.en: After the Twelfth Dynasty Egypt is ruled by a series of short-lived kings. The sources differ about when the Middle Kingdom ends: about 1782, about 1700 or about 1650 BC, depending on how much of the Thirteenth Dynasty is counted. Then follows a new time of fragmentation, when the Hyksos rule northern Egypt.

mapNote.en: The map shows the Middle Kingdom up to and including 1602 BC.

text.en: Ahmose I drives out the Hyksos and founds the Eighteenth Dynasty. Egypt then expands into the Levant and far south into Nubia.

mapNote.en: The map shows the New Kingdom from 1501 BC.

text.en: Thutmose III rules first together with Hatshepsut and then alone. He makes at least 16 campaigns in 20 years and conquers large parts of the Near East, from the Euphrates to Nubia.

mapNote.en: The map shows an increase of about 11 per cent from 1401 BC.

text.en: Ramesses II tries to retake territories in the Levant from the Hittites. The Battle of Kadesh ends in a draw, both sides claim victory, and in the end the empires make peace.
Attacks from Libyans and the Sea Peoples have weakened the empire, and the priests of Amun finally take control of the throne.

mapNote.en: The map shows the New Kingdom up to and including 802 BC, from 1001 BC with about half the area.

The sources give the Old Kingdom as about 2686–2181 BC (World History Encyclopedia about 2613–2181), the Middle Kingdom as about 2055–1650 BC (or to about 1782 or 1700, depending on the definition) and the New Kingdom as about 1570–1069 BC. The map shows the Old Kingdom 2501–2202 BC, the Middle Kingdom 2001–1602 BC and the New Kingdom 1501–802 BC.

summary.en: Assyria was a great power centred on the city of Assur in northern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq. During the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BC) it became the largest empire the world had seen up to then. The map shows both the older Assyria and the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

text.en: The city of Assur was founded about 2600 BC but became independent only around 2025 BC. Under Ashur-uballit I in the 14th century BC the Middle Assyrian Empire emerged. The Neo-Assyrian period is counted from Adad-nirari II's accession in 911 BC; World History Encyclopedia gives 912 BC.
Weakened by civil wars, the empire was conquered by Babylonians and Medes: Assur fell in 614, Nineveh in 612 and Harran in 609 BC. Why such a mighty empire fell so quickly is still debated.
Assur, Nimrud (from 879 BC), Dur-Sharrukin (706–705 BC), Nineveh (705–612 BC) and finally Harran (612–609 BC).

Shamshi-Adad I (about 1808–1776 BC), Tukulti-Ninurta I (about 1243–1207 BC), Ashurnasirpal II (883–859), Tiglath-Pileser III (745–727), Sargon II (722–705), Sennacherib (705–681), Esarhaddon (681–669) and Ashurbanipal (669–631 BC).

Under Esarhaddon, who conquered Egypt in 671 BC. Wikipedia's fact box gives about 1.4 million km² in 670 BC. The empire then ruled all of Mesopotamia, the Levant and Egypt and parts of Anatolia, Arabia and present-day Iran and Armenia.
Akkadian and Imperial Aramaic. Aramaic became the common language of the region, among other reasons because the empire moved parts of conquered peoples to other provinces. Mesopotamian religion.

The empire had a system of roads and relay posts for messengers, and official messages did not travel faster in the Middle East until the 19th century. Ashurbanipal's library, the largest in the history of Mesopotamia, held more than 30,000 documents.
Under Ashur-uballit I Assyria grows from a city-state into a great power, one of the two major empires in Mesopotamia alongside Babylonia.

mapNote.en: The map shows the great growth only from 1301 BC.

text.en: Adad-nirari II becomes king. He and his successors retake the territories in northern Mesopotamia, eastern Anatolia and the Levant that had been lost in the 11th century BC.

mapNote.en: The map shows Assyria as very small in 1001–902 BC and the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 901 BC.

text.en: After a time when generals and officials had ruled, Tiglath-Pileser III restores royal power and more than doubles the empire. He conquers Babylonia and large parts of the Levant.

mapNote.en: The map shows the growth only from 701 BC, when the area almost doubles.

text.en: Esarhaddon conquers Egypt, and the empire reaches its greatest extent. Under Sennacherib the capital had been moved to Nineveh.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire at its largest in 676–617 BC, but without Egypt. Cliopatria shows Assyrian Egypt as a separate area in 651–617 BC, which is not included here.

text.en: Babylonians and Medes take Nineveh. The last king, Ashur-uballit II, holds out in Harran until 609 BC.

mapNote.en: The map shows a greatly reduced empire in 616–602 BC.

The sources give Assyria as an independent state from around 2025 to 609 BC. The map shows Assyria from 1801 BC and the Neo-Assyrian Empire up to and including 602 BC, a few years after the sources' end year.

summary.en: The Neo-Babylonian Empire, also called the Chaldean Empire, was the last empire ruled by kings from ancient Mesopotamia. It had its centre in Babylon and took over large parts of the Assyrian Empire.

text.en: Nabopolassar was crowned king in Babylon in 626 BC. The empire became a great power when, together with the Medes, it overthrew Assyria in 612–609 BC.

The Persian king Cyrus the Great conquered the empire in 539 BC, after the Battle of Opis. The last king, Nabonidus, had favoured the moon god Sin over Babylon's patron god Marduk, and Cyrus presented himself as Marduk's protector.
Babylon.
Nabopolassar (626–605 BC), Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BC) and Nabonidus (556–539 BC).
Under Nebuchadnezzar II. Wikipedia's fact box gives about 500,000 km² in 562 BC.
Akkadian and Imperial Aramaic. Babylonian religion, with Marduk as Babylon's patron god.

Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon with, among other things, the Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way. He besieged Jerusalem in 587 BC, when Solomon's temple was destroyed and the Babylonian captivity began. According to some sources he had the Hanging Gardens of Babylon laid out, but whether they existed at all is debated.
Nabopolassar is crowned king in Babylon, which has long been under Assyrian rule.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire only from 601 BC. Before that Cliopatria shows Babylonia as a separate empire, which is not included here.

text.en: Babylonians and Medes take the Assyrian capital Nineveh. Assyria's last stronghold, Harran, falls in 609 BC.

Nebuchadnezzar defeats Pharaoh Necho II at Carchemish. Shortly afterwards his father dies, and Nebuchadnezzar becomes king. During his 43 years as king Babylon becomes the most powerful empire in the Middle East.
The Babylonians besiege Jerusalem, and Solomon's temple is destroyed. The event begins the Babylonian captivity.
Cyrus the Great defeats the Babylonians at Opis, and the empire falls. The empire had existed for less than a hundred years.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire up to and including 532 BC.
The sources give 626–539 BC. The map shows the empire 601–532 BC. The map's area, about 700,000 km² in 601–552 BC, is larger than the fact box's estimate.

summary.en: Carthage was a city in present-day Tunisia founded by Phoenicians from Tyre. It grew into a trading empire that dominated the western Mediterranean, until Rome destroyed the city in 146 BC.

text.en: Merchants from Tyre, in present-day Lebanon, founded Carthage around 814 BC. According to Wikipedia's text the city became independent in the 7th century BC, after Assyria had conquered Phoenicia; the same article's fact box gives the middle of the 6th century BC.

The conflict with Rome led to the Punic Wars of 264–146 BC. After the second war Carthage lost its fleet and everything except its territory in North Africa. After the third war the Romans destroyed the city in 146 BC.
Carthage.

Carthage was first a monarchy and then became a republic led by suffetes. Hamilcar Barca conquered parts of the Iberian Peninsula in 237–228 BC, and his son Hannibal crossed the Alps during the Second Punic War.

In 300 BC Carthage ruled the north-western coast of North Africa, the southern and eastern Iberian Peninsula and the islands of Sicily (in another place the source says the western half), Sardinia, Corsica, Malta and the Balearic Islands. The source gives no area.
Punic and Punic religion.

Carthage's fleet was one of the largest of antiquity, and the army consisted largely of mercenaries from, among other places, the Iberian Peninsula, Gaul, Greece and North Africa. Almost all Carthaginian texts were destroyed, so most of what we know comes from Greek and Roman authors.

The date palm from Carthage's coins. The horse and the palm were on the coins from the first minting around 410 BC and then throughout the history of the coinage. What they meant is disputed. The most common interpretation of the palm is a pun: the Greek word phoinix means both palm and Phoenician, so the palm showed who minted the coin. The horse is interpreted by some scholars as a god's emblem, and therefore the palm was chosen.
Merchants from the Phoenician city of Tyre found Carthage on the coast of North Africa.

mapNote.en: The map shows Carthage from 651 BC, at first only the city and its immediate surroundings.

text.en: Carthage tries to stop Syracuse from uniting Sicily but loses at Himera, where King Hamilcar dies. Carthage then grows in North Africa and on the Iberian Peninsula instead of in Sicily.

mapNote.en: The map shows Carthage ten times larger already from 501 BC.

text.en: The war against Rome begins. Carthage loses and has to ask for peace, and soon afterwards Rome also takes Sardinia and Corsica.
After the loss to Rome, Hamilcar Barca conquers large parts of the Iberian Peninsula, which is rich in precious metals.

mapNote.en: The map shows the growth from 231 BC.

text.en: Hannibal crosses the Alps and wins great victories in Italy. The Romans under Scipio Africanus finally force him back to Africa, where Carthage loses at Zama and may keep only its territory in North Africa.

mapNote.en: The map shows Carthage at its largest in 219–218 BC and greatly reduced from 203 BC.

text.en: After the Third Punic War the Romans destroy Carthage. Later they found a new city on the site.

mapNote.en: The map shows Carthage up to and including 146 BC.
The sources give about 814–146 BC. The map shows Carthage 651–146 BC.

summary.en: The Seleucid Empire was a Greek state in Western Asia, founded by Alexander the Great's general Seleucus I after Alexander's empire was divided. It was a centre of Hellenistic culture.

text.en: Seleucus I received Babylonia in 321 BC and founded the empire in 312 BC, during the wars between Alexander's generals. He extended it to present-day Iraq, Iran, Afghanistan, Syria and Lebanon.

After the defeat by Rome at Magnesia the empire lost the territories west of the Taurus Mountains, and the Parthians conquered the eastern parts including Mesopotamia. After a civil war a state remained in Syria, which Tigranes the Great of Armenia conquered in 83 BC. The Romans under Pompey ended the empire in 63 BC.
Babylon (312–305 BC), Seleucia (305–240 BC) and Antioch (240–63 BC).
Seleucus I (305–281 BC), Antiochus III the Great and, as the last, Philip II (65–63 BC).

Wikipedia's fact box gives about 3.9 million km² in 301 BC, and then 2.6 million in 240, 800,000 in 175 and 100,000 km² in 100 BC. At its largest the empire comprised Anatolia, Persia, the Levant, Mesopotamia and parts of Central Asia.
Greek was the official language; Old Persian and Aramaic were also spoken. Greek and Babylonian religion, Judaism and Zoroastrianism.

Greek customs and the Greek language were favoured, and a Greek urban elite ruled. The empire repeatedly fought the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt over its western territories. In the east Seleucus concluded an alliance with Chandragupta of the Maurya Empire and ceded territories at the Indus.

The anchor was one of the most common emblems of the Seleucid dynasty, together with the horned horse, the elephant and the goddesses Nike and Tyche. It is found on coins as early as Seleucus I, the founder of the empire.
Seleucus I founds the empire with Babylonia as its base, during the war between Alexander's generals.

mapNote.en: The map shows a small area already in 319–317 BC and then the empire from 308 BC.

text.en: After the Battle of Ipsus the empire is at its largest according to Wikipedia's fact box, about 3.9 million km².

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire at its largest in 302–293 BC, about 3.0 million km².

text.en: Antiochus III the Great takes the war into Greece but is defeated by Rome and its Greek allies at Magnesia. The empire has to pay war reparations and give up its territories west of the Taurus Mountains.

mapNote.en: The map shows a decrease of about 19 per cent from 189 BC.

text.en: The Parthian king Mithridates I takes Media and then Babylonia, where he mints coins at Seleucia in 141 BC.

mapNote.en: The map shows the loss already from 165 BC, when the empire shrinks by about 73 per cent.

text.en: Tigranes the Great of Armenia conquers what remains of the empire in Syria.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire up to and including 79 BC and then again 67–65 BC.

text.en: The Roman general Pompey ends the empire, and Syria becomes a Roman province.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire up to and including 65 BC.
The sources give 312–63 BC. The map shows the empire 319–65 BC, with gaps in 316–309 and 78–68 BC.

summary.en: The Parthian Empire, or the empire of the Arsacids, was an Iranian great power from 247 BC to 224 AD. It lay on the Silk Road between the Roman Empire and the Han Empire and was Rome's great rival in the east.

text.en: Arsaces I led the Parni tribe when they conquered Parthia in north-eastern Iran, a province whose governor had rebelled against the Seleucid Empire. The empire is counted from 247 BC.
Civil war over the throne was more dangerous to the empire than attacks from outside. Ardashir I of Persis rebelled and killed the last king, Artabanus IV, in 224 AD, and founded the Sasanian Empire.
The empire had several capitals. The centre of power moved from Nisa to Ctesiphon on the Tigris, south of present-day Baghdad; Ecbatana, Hecatompylos and Susa were also capitals.
Arsaces I (247–211 BC), Mithridates I (about 171–132 BC), Mithridates II, Orodes II and Artabanus IV (213–224 AD).
From the northern course of the Euphrates, in present-day eastern Turkey, to present-day Afghanistan and western Pakistan. Wikipedia's fact box gives about 2.8 million km² in 1 AD.
Parthian and Greek as official languages, Aramaic as a common language. Zoroastrianism, Babylonian religion and Buddhism.

The Parthians annihilated Crassus's army at Carrhae in 53 BC, one of Rome's worst defeats. The empire grew rich by taxing the caravan trade, among other things in silk, and the Han Empire sent a delegation to Mithridates II's court in 121 BC.

The seated archer with the bow in his hand is found on the reverse of the Parthian kings' coins, from the empire's founder Arsaces I onward. He replaced the god Apollo, who sat with a bow on the Seleucids' coins. Scholars disagree about who the archer is: the king himself or an exalted ancestor of the royal house.
Arsaces I and the Parni conquer Parthia in north-eastern Iran from the Seleucid Empire.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire from 240 BC.

title.en: Mithridates I takes Media and Mesopotamia

text.en: Mithridates I takes Ecbatana in Media in 148 or 147 BC and then conquers Babylonia, where he mints coins at Seleucia in 141 BC.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire seven times larger already from 165 BC.

text.en: The Roman general Crassus invades the empire but is defeated at Carrhae, in present-day south-eastern Turkey. About 20,000 Romans die.
Parthian forces conquer the whole Levant except Tyre from the Romans, but Mark Antony leads a Roman counterattack.

mapNote.en: The map shows only a small increase, about 5 per cent, in 41–38 BC.

text.en: Ardashir I defeats and kills Artabanus IV and founds the Sasanian Empire.

mapNote.en: The map shows a smaller Parthian empire up to and including 237, alongside the Sasanian Empire.
The sources give 247 BC–224 AD. The map shows the empire from 240 BC to 237 AD.

summary.en: The Sasanian Empire was the last Iranian empire before Islam, ruled by the Sasanian dynasty in 224–651. It was the great rival of Rome and Byzantium and a high point of Iranian culture.

text.en: Ardashir I, ruler in Istakhr in Persis, defeated the Parthian king Artabanus IV at the Battle of Hormozdgan in 224 and founded the empire.

A devastating war against Byzantium in 602–628 and four years of civil war weakened the empire. It fell to the Muslim conquests, with defeats at al-Qadisiyya in 636 and Nahavand in 642. The last king, Yazdegerd III, was murdered in Merv in 651.
Istakhr (224–226) and then Ctesiphon (226–637).
Ardashir I (224–241), Shapur I, Khosrow I (531–579), Khosrow II (590–628) and Yazdegerd III (632–651).
Under Khosrow II, whose forces took Jerusalem in 614, Alexandria in 619 and the rest of Egypt in 621. Wikipedia's fact box gives about 3.5 million km² in 550.
Middle Persian. Zoroastrianism was the state religion; in the empire there were also Christians, Manichaeans, Jews and Mazdakites.
Shapur I took the Roman emperor Valerian prisoner at Edessa in 260 and celebrated the victory with rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam. Khosrow I is known for his reforms of taxes and administration.

The Derafsh Kaviani, the royal banner, was the Sasanian Empire's official standard and a sign of royal power. Under the Sasanians it had a star as its emblem and tassels in red, gold and purple. According to legend it was the blacksmith Kaveh's leather apron. When the Arabs captured the banner at the Battle of al-Qadisiyya it became a symbol of the empire's fall.
Ardashir I defeats the Parthian king Artabanus IV and founds the empire.

mapNote.en: The map shows Ardashir's realm already from 215, as a small area in present-day southern Iran.

text.en: Shapur I defeats the Romans at Edessa and takes Emperor Valerian prisoner. He enters Anatolia but withdraws after a defeat.

mapNote.en: The map shows an increase of about 17 per cent in 260–262.

title.en: Khosrow II takes Jerusalem and Egypt

text.en: During the war against Byzantium Persian forces take Jerusalem in 614, Alexandria in 619 and the rest of Egypt in 621. The dream of restoring the Achaemenids' borders is almost fulfilled.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire at its largest in 623–625, close to 5 million km².

text.en: After Emperor Heraclius's counterattack Khosrow II is overthrown by his son Kavad II, who ends the war and gives up all the occupied territories. Four years of civil war follow.

mapNote.en: The map shows a decrease of about 26 per cent from 629.

text.en: The Muslim armies win at al-Qadisiyya in 636 and Nahavand in 642. Yazdegerd III flees east and is murdered in Merv in 651.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire up to and including 643.
The sources give 224–651. The map shows the empire 215–643.

summary.en: Qin was a state in western China under the Zhou dynasty. After extensive reforms it conquered the other warring states and united China in 221 BC. The Qin dynasty became China's first imperial dynasty but lasted only until 206 BC.

text.en: The state of Qin is traditionally dated to 897 BC. It lay on the western edge of Chinese culture, which gave room to grow. In 770 BC Qin received a letter of enfeoffment from King Ping of Zhou.

When Qin Shi Huang died in 210 BC two advisers put an heir on the throne in order to rule themselves. Revolts broke out, and the empire fell to Xiang Yu and Liu Bang, generals from Chu. The capital Xianyang was destroyed in 206 BC, and Liu Bang founded the Han Empire.
The state of Qin moved its capital several times, among other places to Yong. The last was Xianyang, which was also the capital of the Qin dynasty.
Duke Xiao, who supported Shang Yang's reforms in the 4th century BC, King Ying Zheng, who became Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor (221–210 BC), and Qin Er Shi (210–207 BC).
Wikipedia's fact box gives about 2.3 million km² in 220 BC. From 214 BC Qin also advanced south towards the areas where the Baiyue peoples lived.
Old Chinese. Chinese folk religion and ancestor worship.

Qin standardised currency, measures, weights and script, linked walls along the northern border into what would become the Great Wall of China, and built a large road network. Qin Shi Huang's tomb complex is guarded by the Terracotta Army, life-size soldiers.
King Ping of Zhou gives Qin a letter of enfeoffment. For a long time Qin is a lesser power in the west.

mapNote.en: The map shows Qin from 751 BC.

text.en: Qin conquers the states of Ba and Shu in present-day Sichuan. The fertile and hard-to-reach areas give Qin food, soldiers and a base for attacks on Chu.

mapNote.en: The map shows Qin seven times larger from 316 BC.

text.en: King Ying Zheng conquers the rival states one by one. In 221 BC China is united, and he takes the name Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor.

mapNote.en: The map shows the greatest growth in 224–223 BC.

text.en: Qin Shi Huang sends the main part of his army south against the Baiyue peoples. The army loses over 100,000 men but builds a canal to bring up reinforcements.

mapNote.en: The map shows an increase of about 18 per cent from 213 BC.

text.en: After Qin Shi Huang's death revolts break out. Qin surrenders to Liu Bang in 207 BC, and Xianyang is destroyed in 206 BC.

mapNote.en: The map shows the Qin dynasty up to and including 210 BC.
The sources date the state of Qin traditionally to 897 BC and the Qin dynasty to 221–206 BC. The map shows the state of Qin 751–220 BC and the Qin dynasty 219–210 BC.

summary.en: The Gupta Empire was an Indian empire that from the middle of the 3rd century to the middle of the 6th century ruled large parts of northern India. The period has been called India's golden age, but that description is disputed.

text.en: The dynasty was founded by a king called Gupta, about 240–280, in Magadha on the Ganges plain. The great expansion began with Chandragupta I, who was crowned in 320.

The empire lost land and power to its own vassals and was attacked by Huns from Central Asia (Kidarites and Alchon Huns). After Skandagupta's death in 467 it went downhill. The sources differ about the end: Wikipedia gives about 579, World History Encyclopedia about 550.
Pataliputra, and after 455 Ayodhya.
Chandragupta I (from 320), Samudragupta (from about 335 or 350 to about 375), Chandragupta II (375–415), Kumaragupta I (until 455) and Skandagupta (until 467).

The empire grew through Samudragupta's campaigns, and Chandragupta II defeated the Western Satraps in Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra in a campaign that lasted until 409. The sources differ about the area: Wikipedia's fact box gives both about 3.5 million km² in 400 and 1.7 million km² in 440.
Sanskrit in literature and learning, Prakrit in everyday life. Vaishnavism was the official religion, and Buddhism and Jainism also existed. The rulers were Hindus but tolerant of other religions.
The Mahabharata and the Ramayana received their fixed form during the period, and scholars such as the poet Kalidasa and the astronomers Aryabhata and Varahamihira were active here.

Garuda, a mythical bird, was the emblem of the Gupta kings and was on the empire's seals and coins (Garudadhvaja). Garuda is the god Vishnu's mount, and the emblem shows that the Gupta kings worshipped Vishnu. It is used here because the sources expressly call it the empire's royal emblem.
Chandragupta I is crowned and begins a rapid expansion of the empire from Magadha.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire from 324.

text.en: Samudragupta succeeds his father. According to an inscription on the Allahabad Pillar he defeats kings in the north and twelve rulers in the south, along India's east coast.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire eleven times larger from 347.

text.en: Chandragupta II extends the empire westward and defeats the Western Satraps in Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra in a campaign that lasts until 409.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire at its largest in 410–450, about 2.5 million km².

text.en: Skandagupta repels an attack by Huns, but the war drains the empire's resources. The Kidarites seem to have kept the western part of the empire.

mapNote.en: The map shows a decrease of about 11 per cent from 451.

text.en: After Skandagupta's death the empire goes downhill. The coins show that the Gupta kings lose control of large parts of western India after 467–469.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire halved from 490.
The sources give the middle of the 3rd century to about 579 (Wikipedia) or about 550 (World History Encyclopedia). The map shows the empire 324–554, from Chandragupta I's time.

summary.en: Aksum was a kingdom in the Horn of Africa, centred in present-day Eritrea and northern Ethiopia. It was a great power on the trade route between the Roman Empire and India and at times also ruled parts of southern Arabia.

text.en: The kingdom emerged from the older Dʿmt culture and was founded in the first century AD, with the city of Aksum as its capital.

The decline had begun in the 7th century, when coin minting ceased, and the presence of the Persians and later the Muslims in the Red Sea weakened trade. The sources differ about the end: according to Wikipedia the kingdom fell in unclear circumstances around 960, according to World History Encyclopedia it lived on as a much smaller state into the 8th century.
Aksum, and after about 800 Kubar.
Gedara (about 200–230), Endubis (270–310), Ezana (320s to about 360) and Kaleb (514–542).
Under Kaleb, who conquered Himyar in Yemen. Wikipedia gives about 2.5 million km² in 525 and 1.25 million km² in 350.

Ge’ez, Sabaean and Greek. Christianity became the state religion under Ezana; before that several gods were worshipped. The sources date the conversion differently, to 325 or 328 (Wikipedia's fact box) and around 350 (World History Encyclopedia).

Aksum was the first kingdom south of the Sahara to mint its own coins, and the coins have been found as far away as Caesarea and southern India. Mani, the founder of Manichaeism, counted Aksum among the four great powers of the 3rd century, together with Persia, Rome and China.
From the older Dʿmt culture a kingdom emerges with the city of Aksum as its capital.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire already from 51 BC.

text.en: King Ezana makes Christianity the state religion and for a short time conquers Meroë in Kush, in 330. Aksum then inherits the Greek name Ethiopia. The sources date the conversion to 325 or 328, or around 350.

At the request of the Byzantine emperor Justin I, Kaleb attacks Himyar in Yemen to stop King Dhu Nuwas's persecution of Christians, and the empire reaches its greatest extent. According to the source Aksum keeps southern Arabia only until 525, when Abraha takes power.

mapNote.en: The map shows the area in Yemen only in 534–601.

text.en: In the wars against Persia Aksum loses its territories in Arabia.

mapNote.en: The map shows the area in Yemen up to and including 601.

text.en: The empire's last three centuries are regarded as a dark age, and it falls in unclear circumstances around 960. World History Encyclopedia says instead that the empire lived on as a smaller state into the 8th century.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire up to and including 946.

The sources give the first century AD to around 960 (Wikipedia) or into the 8th century (World History Encyclopedia). The map shows the empire 51 BC–946 AD. The map's area, mostly about 100,000 km², is much smaller than Wikipedia's estimates.

summary.en: The Umayyad Caliphate was the second Islamic caliphate, ruled by the Umayyad family from Damascus. Under the Umayyads the early Muslim conquests continued, and the empire became one of the largest in history.

text.en: Mu'awiya, who had long been governor of Syria, became caliph in 661 after winning the first civil war (the First Fitna). He succeeded the Rashidun Caliphate and made rule hereditary in his own family. Syria became the empire's core land.

The constant wars drained the empire's resources, and revolts and rivalry between tribes weakened it from within. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew the last caliph, Marwan II, and most of the Umayyad family were killed. A grandson of Caliph Hisham, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped and in 756 founded a realm of his own in al-Andalus with Córdoba as its capital.
Damascus (661–744) and Harran (744–750).
Mu'awiya I (661–680), the first; Abd al-Malik, who won the second civil war in 692 and made the administration more centralised; and Marwan II (744–750), the last.

About 11–15 million km² around the year 720, according to Wikipedia. The empire then stretched from the Maghreb and the Iberian Peninsula to Central Asia and Sindh. The map data (Cliopatria) gives at most about 9.9 million km² in the 730s and 740s.

Language: Arabic (official). Religion: Islam as the state religion. Christians, who were still a majority of the population, and Jews were allowed to practise their religion on payment of the jizya tax. The Umayyads' best-known buildings are the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed in 691/692, and the Great Mosque of Damascus.
The white banner. The Umayyads' banners were white, after Muawiya's banner, and white was the dynasty's colour. The banner is shown without text.
Mu'awiya wins the first civil war and becomes caliph. Damascus becomes the capital, and the Umayyads' hereditary rule begins.

mapNote.en: The map shows the caliphate as a large empire only from 666. Before that Cliopatria counts most of it as the Rashidun Caliphate, which is not included here.

text.en: Abd al-Malik defeats the Zubayrids and regains control of the whole caliphate. He makes the administration more centralised and introduces Arabic and Islam into the bureaucracy. The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem is completed in 691/692.

mapNote.en: The map shows a smaller area in 682–691 and grows again in 692.

title.en: The Iberian Peninsula, Sindh and Central Asia

text.en: Tariq ibn Ziyad enters the Visigothic Kingdom in 711, and within five years most of the Iberian Peninsula is conquered. From 708/709 Sindh in India is conquered, and in 711–712 Qutayba takes Khwarazm and Samarkand in Central Asia.

mapNote.en: The map shows the Iberian Peninsula only from 718. The map data does not count Bukhara and Samarkand as part of the caliphate.

text.en: The Franks under Charles Martel defeat an Umayyad army at Tours, and the expansion in the west comes to a halt. The last fortress north of the Pyrenees, Narbonne, is lost in 759.
The Abbasids defeat Caliph Marwan II at the river Zab and overthrow the Umayyads. Most of the Umayyad family are killed.

mapNote.en: The map data shows the Iberian Peninsula as Umayyad in 751–756, before Abd al-Rahman I founds his realm in Córdoba in 756.
The sources give 661–750. The map data (Cliopatria) runs 656–756: Mu'awiya's Syria already during the civil war of 656–661 and the Iberian Peninsula in 751–756.

summary.en: The Abbasid Caliphate was the third Islamic caliphate, ruled by a dynasty descended from Muhammad's uncle Abbas. The capital Baghdad became a centre of science and culture during what is called the Islamic Golden Age.

text.en: The Abbasid Revolution began in Khurasan, far from the Umayyads' Syria, and overthrew the Umayyads in 750. The caliph first ruled from Kufa in Iraq.

In the 9th century many provinces became self-governing under dynasties of their own, and in the 10th century the caliph became a figurehead. Real power lay with the Buyids, who took Baghdad in 945, and the Seljuks, who took the city in 1055. The Abbasids took back Iraq in the 12th century, but in 1258 the Mongols under Hulagu sacked Baghdad and executed the caliph al-Musta'sim. A branch of the family were caliphs without political power in Cairo under the Mamluks in 1261–1517.
Kufa (750–762), Baghdad (762–836 and 892–1258) and Samarra (836–892). The shadow caliphs of 1261–1517 sat in Cairo.

al-Saffah (750–754), the first; al-Mansur, who founded Baghdad in 762; Harun al-Rashid (786–809), whose time is regarded as the Abbasids' high point; and al-Musta'sim (1242–1258), the last caliph in Baghdad.
The map data (Cliopatria) gives at most about 8.1 million km² in the second half of the 8th century. After that the empire shrinks, most sharply in 875 and 899.

Language: Arabic (official). Religion: Islam as the state religion, with Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians as minorities. In Baghdad there was the centre of learning the House of Wisdom. After a civil war in the 9th century the caliphs built up a professional army of mainly Turkish slave soldiers.

The black banner. The Abbasids' revolt against the Umayyads in 747 took place under black banners, and after the victory in 750 the Abbasids kept black as the dynasty's colour, on banners and on the caliphs' clothing, as a contrast to the Umayyads' white. The banner is shown here without text.
The Abbasids defeat the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, at the river Zab. al-Saffah is proclaimed caliph in Kufa.

mapNote.en: The map shows a smaller area in 750 and the whole empire from 751.

text.en: Caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad on the Tigris and makes the city the capital. It becomes a centre of science, culture and art.
After the civil war and with the new army of Turkish slave soldiers, the caliph builds a new capital, Samarra. The caliph's seat moves back to Baghdad in 892.
In the 9th century local dynasties take over in the provinces, among them the Aghlabids, Tahirids, Samanids, Saffarids and Tulunids.

mapNote.en: The map shows large decreases in 875 and 899.

text.en: The Iranian Buyid dynasty takes Baghdad. The caliph becomes a figurehead, and real power lies with the Buyids and from 1055 with the Seljuks.

mapNote.en: The map data shows the Buyids' rule in Baghdad as a separate part, the Abbasid Caliphate under the Buyids, in 947–969. Between 970 and 1201 Cliopatria lacks the Abbasid Caliphate entirely.

text.en: The Mongols under Hulagu sack Baghdad and execute the caliph al-Musta'sim. It becomes in practice the end of the caliphate.

mapNote.en: The map data shows the Abbasids in Iraq in 1202–1259.
The sources give 750–1258, and after that shadow caliphs in Cairo until 1517. The map data (Cliopatria) runs 750–969, lacks the caliphate in 970–1201 and shows it again in Iraq in 1202–1259.

summary.en: The Frankish Empire was the largest empire in Western Europe after the fall of the Western Roman Empire. It was founded by Clovis I and ruled by the Merovingians and then the Carolingians. Under Charlemagne it became an empire over large parts of Western and Central Europe.

text.en: Frankish tribes on the Rhine and the Meuse spread out into Roman Gaul. Clovis I became king around 481 and united the Franks, but exactly when he became king of all the Franks is unknown. He took Soissons in 486 and Aquitaine in 507 and made Paris the capital in 508.

The empire was often divided among the king's sons. After the death of Louis the Pious in 840 it was divided in 843 by the Treaty of Verdun into West Francia, Middle Francia and East Francia. West Francia became France under the Capetians; the last Frankish king there, Louis V, died in 987. East Francia became the Kingdom of Germany, the core of the Holy Roman Empire.
Paris under Clovis I (from 508). His sons had their capitals in Reims, Orléans, Paris and Soissons. Charlemagne built a large palace in Aachen, which WHE calls his capital.
Clovis I (about 481–511), Pepin the Short, the first Carolingian king (751–768), Charlemagne (768–814, emperor from 800) and Louis the Pious (died 840).
About 1.2 million km² in 814, according to Wikipedia's fact box. The map data (Cliopatria) gives at most about 1.3 million km² in 806–813.

Religion: Catholic Christianity. Clovis I converted to Catholicism; the baptism is traditionally dated to 496 but is now thought to have taken place in 508. Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in Rome on Christmas Day in the year 800.
Clovis I defeats Syagrius, the last Roman ruler in Gaul, and takes Soissons. With that he rules all of northern Gaul.
Clovis defeats the Visigoths at Vouillé and takes their land north of the Pyrenees, except Septimania.

mapNote.en: The map shows the large increase from 510.

text.en: The Franks under Charles Martel defeat an Umayyad army at Tours, and the Umayyads' advance in Europe comes to a halt.

mapNote.en: The map shows the empire growing sharply in 732.

text.en: Pepin the Short deposes the last Merovingian king, Childeric III, and becomes king. The Carolingian era begins.

mapNote.en: The map data switches from the Merovingians to the Carolingians already in 718.

text.en: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor in Rome on Christmas Day. The empire becomes the Carolingian Empire.

mapNote.en: The map shows Charlemagne's conquests as increases in 775 and 788.

text.en: Louis the Pious's three sons divide the empire into West Francia, Middle Francia and East Francia.

mapNote.en: The map data counts all the parts as the empire until 910 and after that mainly West Francia.

title.en: The last Carolingian in the west

text.en: Louis V, the last Frankish king in West Francia, dies. The kingdom passes to the Capetians and becomes France.

mapNote.en: The map data ends in 989.

Wikipedia gives about 481–843 for the Frankish Empire as a whole. WHE gives the Merovingians as about 481–751 and the Carolingians as 751–887. The map data (Cliopatria) runs 462–989 and switches from the Merovingians to the Carolingians already in 718.

summary.en: The Holy Roman Empire was a loosely held-together empire in Central and Western Europe, led by an elected emperor. For a long time it consisted of the kingdoms of Germany, Italy and Burgundy and existed for almost a thousand years, until 1806.

text.en: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in the year 800, but the title had lapsed again by 924. It was revived in 962, when Pope John XII crowned Otto I, king of Germany, emperor. Some historians count the empire from 800, others from 962.
Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine of German states that sided with France. On 6 August 1806 Emperor Francis II abdicated and dissolved the empire.

No fixed capital. The kings were often elected and crowned in Frankfurt and Aachen, and Charles IV made Prague the emperor's seat. Vienna became the capital of the Habsburgs' hereditary lands, but not of the empire.
Otto I (962–973), Frederick III (1452–1493), Charles V (1519–1556) and the last, Francis II (1792–1806).

The empire had its greatest extent and power in the middle of the 13th century, under the House of Hohenstaufen. Wikipedia's fact box gives about 1.1 million km² in 1150. The map data (Cliopatria) gives at most about 1.2 million km² in 1450–1458, when it also counts Hungary as part of the empire.

Language: German and medieval Latin (administration, church and ceremonies), and many others. Religion: Latin Christianity, and after the Reformation several official religions. The emperor was elected by prince-electors, both secular princes and archbishops. From 1512 the empire was also called the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation.

The imperial eagle, a black eagle on a golden field, was the arms of the emperors and the empire. In the Middle Ages the eagle usually had one head, as on the map. From Emperor Sigismund in 1433 the double-headed eagle became the empire's arms until the end in 1806.
Pope John XII crowns Otto I, king of Germany and Italy, emperor in Rome. This is most often counted as the beginning of the empire.

mapNote.en: The map data shows the empire already from 922, with the Kingdom of Germany before 962.

title.en: Burgundy becomes part of the empire

text.en: Conrad II incorporates the Kingdom of Burgundy. The empire now consists of three kingdoms: Germany, Italy and Burgundy. Wikipedia gives both 1032 and 1033.

mapNote.en: The map data counts Burgundy (the Kingdom of Arles) as part of the empire already from 1010.

text.en: Emperor Charles IV issues the Golden Bull. It lays down that seven prince-electors elect the emperor and remains in force until 1806.
The peace ends the Thirty Years' War. The Habsburgs remain emperors, but their power is increasingly limited to their own Austrian, Bohemian and Hungarian lands.

mapNote.en: From 1648 the map no longer shows Switzerland and the United Netherlands. The Peace of Westphalia made Switzerland formally independent; for the Netherlands the sources give different years (1581, 1648 or 1653).

text.en: Emperor Francis II abdicates and dissolves the empire, after Napoleon has created the Confederation of the Rhine.

mapNote.en: The sources give 962–1806, and some historians count from 800. The map data (Cliopatria) begins in 922 with the Kingdom of Germany. In 1450–1458 Cliopatria also counts Hungary and the Teutonic Order's Prussia as part of the empire, although they never belonged to it, and that is why the empire is at its largest on the map just then. From 1459 Cliopatria counts only the small states as part of the empire and shows the large states as empires of their own.
